source: Wang, Zhang, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky (2023/2024) Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making
finding: Bridge uses cognitive task analysis with expert teachers to turn latent reasoning into a 3-step decision model (A infer the student error, B pick a strategy, C pick an intention). Feeding the expert's decisions to GPT-4 makes its tutoring replies much better liked by raters.
numbers: CTA with 4 experienced math teachers; 700 real tutoring conversations (grades 1-5). GPT-4 with expert decisions vs no decisions: +76% on 'prefer', +80% on 'useful'; overall score 0.83 vs 0.51 (expert-written reply 1.02). Raters were teachers recruited via Prolific.
quote: models of expert decision making critical to closing the gap
limits: Only 4 experts, US only. Rated by teachers, not by student learning. Zero-shot greedy decoding. Abstract says random decisions cost -97% vs expert, the intro says -67%; the paper disagrees with itself.
agent_relevance: A CTA-derived decision scaffold (notice, strategy, intention) is a concrete, tested lesson format. A good model for storing what an expert noticed and why they acted.

source: Wang, Zhang, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky (2023/2024) Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making (self-selected decisions)
finding: Models can pick their own decisions in the same 3-step form, but only some gain. GPT-4 and Llama-2 improve; GPT-3.5 does not because its own decisions are poor.
numbers: Self-decision overall: GPT-4 0.84, Llama-2 0.70, GPT-3.5 0.16 (no-decision baseline: 0.51, 0.53, 0.28). Gains on 'prefer'/'useful' up to +95% for GPT-4 and Llama-2 (p<0.05).
limits: GPT-3.5 self-decisions collapsed onto few strategies (decision-path analysis). Expert condition did not raise the 'care' score for Llama-2 or GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: A scaffold step can be filled by the agent itself, but only if the base model is strong enough. Gate the step on model capability.

source: Wang, Zhang, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky (2023/2024) Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making (diversity and random control)
finding: Expert decision paths are diverse; LLM decision paths are narrow. Random decisions hurt, so the benefit comes from choosing the decision to fit the context, not from extra structure alone.
numbers: Path entropy: experts 6.00, GPT-4 3.37. Random-decision GPT-4 overall 0.26 vs 0.83 with expert decisions and 0.51 with none (p<0.05 vs expert).
limits: Entropy is a coarse measure. Random decisions are a harsh control.
agent_relevance: Structure without context-sensitive selection can be worse than no structure. A lesson library needs retrieval that fits the case.

source: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky (2024, rev. 2026) Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
finding: Deployed form of the Bridge CTA method: a tutor-facing LLM tool giving expert-like suggestions. First preregistered randomized trial of a human-AI system in live tutoring. Students of tutors with the tool were more likely to pass exit tickets.
numbers: n=783 tutors analysed, 1,013 students, 4,136 sessions, 350,000+ messages. Pass rate 62% to 66% (+4 pp, p<0.01). +9 pp for students of lower-rated tutors. Cost about $20 per tutor per year.
quote: models expert thinking to assist tutors in real time
limits: Outcome is exit-ticket mastery; estimated test-score effect is small (about 0.024 SD). One provider, one district, math only. Message classifiers had agreement between 0.65 and 0.90 on a 3,000 message sample.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that a CTA-built scaffold carries through to real outcomes. Effects were biggest for the weakest performers, which matters if our agent runs on a weaker base model.

source: Du, Jiang, Shen, Ren (2019) Eliciting Knowledge from Experts: Automatic Transcript Parsing for Cognitive Task Analysis
finding: Early NLP attempt to automate the costly step of CTA: turning interview transcripts into structured protocols (flowcharts with next and if relations). Weakly supervised, with fuzzy matching, sequence labeling and span-pair relation extraction.
numbers: Fuzzy matching best 47.1% mention-level accuracy; best sequence labeling 38.18% token accuracy; best span-pair relation extraction 74.4% micro F1. Manual test set of 138 protocol phrases.
limits: Pre-LLM (BERT era), small data, noisy supervision. Low accuracy for extracting the actions themselves.
agent_relevance: Shows the bottleneck: transcript to structured knowledge. Modern LLMs could do it, but no measured LLM successor was found in this search.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE)
finding: Models that interview the user (open questions, yes/no questions, edge cases) elicit what the user wants better than the user's own written prompt in many settings. This is machine-run elicitation, close to a CTA interview.
numbers: Preregistered, 388 participants, 3 domains (email validation, content recommendation, moral reasoning). GATE beat user-written prompts in 6/10 settings on absolute score and 7/10 on time-normalised AUC; generative yes/no questions beat prompts in every setting. Users found it less mentally demanding.
limits: Significance only in content recommendation and email domains; low power in moral reasoning. Elicits preferences, not expert reasoning.
agent_relevance: Interview-by-model can surface considerations the user did not think of. Supports an elicitation step before the agent acts.

source: Li et al. (2023) GATE: model-simulated respondents versus humans
finding: Model-simulated respondents track human results in two of three domains, so cheap pilots of an elicitation protocol are possible but not safe everywhere.
numbers: Model-model AUC and change-after-5-turns correlated with human results in content recommendation and email validation; not in moral reasoning.
limits: Correlation was weaker in the subjective domain. Simulated experts may not capture tacit knowledge.
agent_relevance: Do not trust an LLM stand-in expert to validate a CTA protocol in judgment-heavy domains.

source: Andukuri, Fraenken, Gerstenberg, Goodman (2024) STaR-GATE: Teaching Language Models to Ask Clarifying Questions
finding: Self-training a model to ask more useful questions improves the final answers it gives. A questioner learns to elicit a hidden persona's preferences.
numbers: 25,500 synthetic persona-task prompts. After 2 iterations responses preferred over the initial model on 72% of tasks (GPT-4 judge). With other Roleplayers the win rate dropped to 65% and 62%; a llama3-8b setup gave 66%.
limits: Win rate falls when the Roleplayer changes; one ablation shows rates falling back to 50%. Trained on simulated personas, not real experts.
agent_relevance: Asking good questions is learnable, but gains are tied to the simulated respondent. Question quality is the weak point of interview methods.

source: Wuttke et al. (2024) AI Conversational Interviewing: Transforming Surveys with LLMs as Adaptive Interviewers
finding: A GPT-4 turbo interviewer was compared to human student interviewers with the same questionnaire. Data quality was comparable, but failure types differ: humans skip active listening, the model skips follow-up probes.
numbers: Guideline violations per interview 72 (AI) vs 64 (human). 94% of active-listening violations were by humans (6% AI). 88% of violations of the 'ask a follow-up when an answer is surprising or unclear' rule were by the AI. Small seminar pilot (sample count not recovered).
limits: Small student sample, political topics, not expert decision interviews. A small prompt change broke follow-up behaviour that worked in pretests.
agent_relevance: Probing is the step CDM depends on (deepening sweeps). LLM interviewers under-probe; this needs an explicit probe scaffold and a test after every prompt edit.

source: Wuttke et al. (2024) AI Conversational Interviewing: instruction sensitivity
finding: The model interviewer followed the follow-up rule in internal pretests but broke it in the main study after small prompt edits.
numbers: 88% of follow-up-rule violations came from the AI; the paper notes pretests had succeeded.
limits: Single study; cause not isolated.
agent_relevance: Prompt fragility in elicitation behaviour: add a test per rule (such as probing) in any interviewing agent.

source: Savage et al. (2023) Diagnostic Reasoning Prompts Reveal the Potential for Large Language Model Interpretability in Medicine
finding: Prompts that copy clinicians' named reasoning modes (intuitive, analytic, differential diagnosis, Bayesian) were tested on MedQA against plain chain of thought. A strong model can follow them without losing accuracy; a weak one is hurt.
numbers: GPT-3.5: CoT 46%, intuitive 48% (n.s.), analytic 40% (p=0.001), differential diagnosis 38% (p<0.001), Bayesian 42% (p=0.02). GPT-4 (497 questions): CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, differential 78%, analytic 78%, Bayesian 72% (-3.4%, p=0.07). Rater kappa 0.93 and 0.98.
limits: Reasoning modes come from clinical teaching, not elicited from experts in this study. No accuracy gain for GPT-4, only interpretability.
agent_relevance: Expert reasoning templates do not raise accuracy by themselves and can hurt weak models. Value is in auditability, which fits a thinking schema.

source: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee, Jurgens (2024) Is 'A Helpful Assistant' the Best Role for LLMs? Personas in System Prompts
finding: Telling a model to act as an expert (a cheap stand-in for expert knowledge) does not reliably improve factual accuracy. This is the null control for any 'be the expert' prompt versus real CTA-derived content.
numbers: 162 personas (6 relationship types, 8 expertise domains), 4 LLM families, 2,410 factual questions: adding a persona did not improve over the no-persona control on average. A domain classifier to pick a persona per question had 78.1% accuracy.
quote: adding personas in system prompts does not improve model performance across a range of questions
limits: Factual MMLU-style questions only. Picking the best persona per question after the fact is an oracle, not a method.
agent_relevance: Expert labels on a prompt are not expert knowledge. Real gains in Bridge came from explicit decision content, not a role name.

source: Xu et al. (2023) ExpertPrompting: Instructing Large Language Models to be Distinguished Experts
finding: Auto-written expert identity descriptions per question raised answer quality as judged by GPT-4 in that paper. Contrasts with the persona null result.
numbers: ExpertLLaMA reached 96% of ChatGPT capability by GPT-4 evaluation (abstract figure only).
limits: Judged by GPT-4, not humans or ground truth; only the abstract was read. Not independent replication.
agent_relevance: Per-task detailed expert identity may help where a flat persona does not; unproven.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: An agent that extracts natural-language insights from its own successes and failures (a lessons library) and retrieves similar past trajectories improves on baselines. This is automated lesson building without an expert interview.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieve-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%, WebShop 37% vs 38%. HotpotQA ExpeL 40% vs Reflexion 39% (R3); ALFWorld ExpeL 54% vs Reflexion 59%. ALFWorld retrieve-only rose 40.3% to 54.4% over Reflexion rounds R0-R3.
limits: Which source (insights or trajectories) helps is task dependent. Better insight LLM gave better results.
agent_relevance: Rule-like insights suit reasoning tasks; trajectories suit action tasks. Mix both in a lesson store.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: human-crafted versus LLM-generated insights ablation
finding: Direct ablation of hand-written rules against machine-extracted ones for the same task. Hand-crafted insights beat ReAct but lost to LLM-generated insights; adding reflections to the insight step lowered scores (hallucinated reflections).
numbers: HotpotQA ablation (Table 3); exact table values not extracted here.
limits: One environment, one hand-crafting effort.
agent_relevance: Hand-written expert lessons are not automatically better than machine ones. Test each lesson, not its source.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Inducing reusable workflows from past experience and giving them to a web agent raised success. A workflow is a compressed expert routine, the same object a CTA protocol produces.
numbers: WebArena (GPT-4): +12.0 abs points and +51.1% relative over BrowserGym baseline; about 2.0 fewer steps per task. Mind2Web cross-task: +24.6% relative step success.
limits: Online induction depends on test-time success judgments. WebArena result is one model.
agent_relevance: Induced workflows can replace manually written ones. Suggests CTA-style extraction can be partly automated from trajectories.

source: Wang et al. (2024) AWM versus human-written workflows (SteP)
finding: AWM was compared against SteP, an agent that uses human-expert-written workflows.
numbers: AWM on WebArena overall success is 7.6% relative above SteP.
limits: Different base harness for the two systems; relative gain only.
agent_relevance: Same point as ExpeL: machine-induced routines can match or beat manual expert writing, at least for web tasks.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Distills strategies from both successful and failed trajectories into a memory. Failure lessons add value that success-only methods (Synapse, AWM) miss.
numbers: WebArena overall SR, no memory / ReasoningBank / +MaTTS: Gemini-2.5-flash 40.5 / 48.8 / 51.8; Gemini-2.5-pro 46.7 / 53.9 / 56.3; Claude-3.7-sonnet 41.7 / 46.3 / 48.8. AWM got 44.1, 47.6, 40.8.
limits: AWM fell below no-memory on Claude-3.7-sonnet (40.8 vs 41.7). Self-judged success labels can be wrong. Lessons come from agent runs, not experts.
agent_relevance: Mining failures matches CDM's focus on difficult incidents. Memory from failures is a measured win.

source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky, Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory
finding: A persistent self-curated cheatsheet of strategies and code at inference time lifts accuracy on math and puzzle tasks.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 23.3% to 50.0%; AIME 2025 +30%; GPT-4o Game of 24 10% to 99%; GPQA-Diamond +9%.
limits: Biggest gains come from stored code solutions on tasks with reusable procedures. No human experts involved.
agent_relevance: Where a task has a reusable procedure, a stored lesson can transform results. Reusable code or rules gain most.

source: Selby et al. (2024) Had enough of experts? Quantitative knowledge retrieval from large language models
finding: LLMs were used as stand-in experts to elicit prior distributions for Bayesian models and to impute missing data.
numbers: Abstract reports improved predictive accuracy and reduced data needs on diverse datasets (no single figure read).
limits: Only part of the text was checked. Quantitative priors, not decision cues.
agent_relevance: A machine stand-in for expert elicitation is workable for numbers; unproven for cue-level tacit knowledge.

source: Cervera (2026) Expert Mind: A Retrieval-Augmented Architecture for Expert Knowledge Preservation in the Energy Sector
finding: A proposed RAG system that captures expert knowledge through structured interviews and think-aloud sessions, then answers queries. Design paper with targets, no completed evaluation.
numbers: Planned targets: response fidelity above 85% by expert review, correction rate below 10%. No measured results.
limits: Single independent author, system not evaluated, status 'submitted'. Retrieval turns interviews into documents, not decision models.
agent_relevance: Shows the common pattern: interview to vector store. This loses the cue-action structure CTA is meant to capture.

source: Benderoth et al. (2025) Socially Interactive Agents for Preserving and Transferring Tacit Knowledge in Organizations
finding: A position paper arguing LLM-driven interactive agents can act as knowledge-transfer facilitators who elicit tacit knowledge. Lists requirements and risks.
numbers: No experimental numbers.
limits: Concept paper; no test with experts or learners.
agent_relevance: Confirms interest but no published measured LLM-run CTA was found in this search.

source: Joyner and Vaughn-Cooke (2026) DECIDE-CTA: structured cognitive task analyses from product instructions (MethodsX)
finding: A rule-based method with fixed sentence syntax to write CTAs from product instructions, aimed at non-psychologists. Notes that CTA output varies with the analyst and suggests LLMs could automate drafting.
numbers: Built from reviewed taxonomy literature (22 publications) and a Python script over instruction documents; verb-level agreement set at 33.3% inter-list. No LLM test.
limits: LLM automation is only proposed. Validation was embedded in design phases, not a separate test.
agent_relevance: Names analyst variability as the core CTA reliability problem. A fixed syntax could make LLM-written CTA checkable.

source: Stanik, Puhlfuerss, Mahler, Sasu, Reip, Maalej (2022) Lessons Learned from Customizing and Applying ACTA to Design a Novel Device for Emergency Medical Care
finding: Applied ACTA in four stages (task diagram, knowledge audit, simulation interview and workshop, mockup refinement) with emergency staff. Critics' claim that ACTA is less comprehensive and superficial held in the simulation stage, but it still added useful details.
numbers: Eleven subject-matter experts in the knowledge audit; hierarchical task diagram from two semi-structured interviews.
limits: Case study in one domain; not a controlled test of ACTA's effect. Human-only.
agent_relevance: Gives a staged template and realistic effort levels that an LLM-run interview could follow or replace.

source: Verostek, Griston, Botello, Zwickl (2022) Making expert processes visible: how and why theorists use assumptions and analogies in their research
finding: CTA with semi-structured interviews (protocol inspired by CDM and ACTA) on theoretical physicists. They describe assumptions and analogies as core, repeated steps.
numbers: N=11 theorists.
limits: Small sample, interview self-report; physics only.
agent_relevance: A recent example of CTA applied to scientific reasoning, where cues are assumption-making and analogy use. Relevant to science-style thinking schemas.

source: Leu and Abbass (2018) A Multi-Disciplinary Review of Knowledge Acquisition Methods: From Human to Autonomous Eliciting Agents
finding: Reviews knowledge acquisition across human, human-inspired and autonomous machine agents. Treats the first two as CTA exercises and the third as machine discovery; proposes red-teaming and co-evolution as a fourth category.
numbers: Qualitative review; classification of methods, no pooled numbers.
limits: Pre-LLM. Taxonomic only. Only the opening sections were read.
agent_relevance: Frame for a machine-run CTA agent: a human-inspired eliciting agent, with machine discovery as an alternative route.

source: Search coverage note for angle C (this run)
finding: No measured study was found that runs a full CTA or Critical Decision Method interview with an LLM interviewer and scores the resulting expert knowledge. Closest: Bridge/Tutor CoPilot (human CTA, LLM use) and GATE/AI interviewing (LLM interviewer, non-expert topics).
numbers: Search used arXiv abs and search pages, Crossref and Europe PMC. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv API returned HTTP 429, and the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so coverage is partial.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search; 2025-2026 work may exist.
agent_relevance: The gap may be real: plan a small in-house test of an LLM-run CDM interview versus a human one, scored by expert review.
